title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Dementia Patient—It's the Caregiver Who Gets Dragged Down
dek: The difficulty of dementia care lies not in the patient's condition itself but in the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses and forces post-90s to quit their jobs. Love is a starting point but not a support, and the system hasn't caught these families yet.
why: This isn't a health科普 for the elderly, but a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia families: no standard answers, only realities you must see before it's too late.
who: Only children born in the 80s and 90s, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they haven't made any eldercare arrangements; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care resource gap eventually falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, 23% of the total population; 35 million are disabled elderly, yet there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap isn't absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China accounts for nearly 30% of global cases, and the host estimates that on average one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this may be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies are unreliable
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia mostly comes from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the professor's incontinence in Still Alice is just one form. He met an elderly man who, despite dementia from his tailor background, would still notice stains on visitors' clothes and teach them to remove them with orange peel; he also saw a woman disabled by a car accident who could only hum Liuyang River with focused expression. Dementia covers various causes like Alzheimer's and vascular dementia; each person's life imprint remains in different ways, and care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal depends on national care insurance
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents live like ordinary people, shopping at the supermarket and going to cafes, while staff pose as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose its low replicability—the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over €18 million, of which €17.8 million was covered by the government, and residents' costs are also covered by long-term care-related systems. In contrast, what Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home was the opposite: elevators had to be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease differs not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough; sacrifice drags down caregivers
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between 'I love my mom and dad very much' and 'I'm about to be dragged down by them.' Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse has to learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit their job due to caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers themselves become patients.

points.h: The more you see, the less confident you feel about eldercare
points.body: Having studied eldercare for years, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his own parents' care. He is a first-generation only child, and his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less sure he is; his research assistant even said after each interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how to arrange care for her own parents. Multi-child families also have friction: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and one person who moved their parents to Shenzhen found that rent, medical costs, and nanny fees added up faster than their retirement wages rose. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child independently.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who initially could paint blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later only dared to praise others, afraid to put brush to paper; another woman's husband reported new losses weekly: his wife couldn't recognize their daughter's newborn grandson, not knowing where this child came from. This daily, irreversible downward slide drains caregivers more than physical disability. The long duration of care is not repetitive hardship but facing a small farewell every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived but doesn't cover all elderly
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016 and expanded to about 90 cities by around 2025, with the official pace aiming for universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that long-term care insurance doesn't give money to every elderly person; through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care and meal delivery services; those with mild conditions may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home is often equated with filial impiety in China, and elderly people, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair would fall out within a month. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the proportion choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap won't disappear automatically.

So I think care should be a kind of relationship. In this relationship, I think both the caregiver and the care recipient undergo great changes in identity, emotions, and even the pace of life.
It's like riding a slide—you're going downhill. So at this moment, I think this kind of care is indeed long.
I think although love is a very important foundation, it should not be the only condition for care. It still requires some external resources, including social support, and so on.

Although the more I see and the more cases I encounter, it doesn't mean I have a very complete or perfect plan for my parents' future care. Precisely because I've seen so many different stories, it actually leaves me with more confusion.
